additional_requirements: Functioning is not markedly impaired apart from the impact of the delusion(s) or its ramifications

S019.name: Delusions
S019.description: Fixed beliefs that do not change easily, even in the face of contradictory evidence.

subtypes.Persecutory Delusions: The false belief that one is being harmed or monitored by other people or organizations.
subtypes.Referential Delusions: The conviction that ordinary events, remarks, or behaviors have specific relevance to oneself.
subtypes.Grandiose Delusions: The false belief that one possesses special abilities, power, or fame.
subtypes.Erotomanic Delusions: The false belief that another person is in love with or has affection for them.
subtypes.Nihilistic Delusions: A destructive or negative conviction that the world is ending or that a major catastrophe will occur.
subtypes.Somatic Delusions: The baseless conviction that there is a serious abnormality with one's body or organs.
subtypes.Jealous Delusions: The conviction that one's spouse or romantic partner is being unfaithful without sufficient evidence.

symptom.disease_info: Delusional Disorder is characterized by the presence of one or more persistent, non-bizarre or less clearly bizarre delusions lasting at least one month, in the absence of prominent hallucinations, disorganized thinking, or marked mood episodes that would suggest schizophrenia or a mood disorder with psychotic features. Outside of the delusional beliefs, overall functioning is often relatively preserved, and behavior may appear largely appropriate, which can delay recognition and treatment. The content of the delusions is typically systematized and circumscribed (e.g., persecutory, jealous, somatic, grandiose, or erotomanic themes), and individuals may seek legal, medical, or interpersonal “solutions” to issues stemming from the fixed beliefs. The course is usually chronic, with limited insight and resistance to contradictory evidence, and it is differentiated from obsessive-compulsive or overvalued ideas by the degree of conviction and imperviousness to reasoning.

patient.personality: Michelle is a chronically worried but imaginative and meticulous young woman who channels her energy into highly organized art-making and community-focused creative projects.
patient.stressor: Michelle’s difficulties began in the months following a chaotic, short-lived marriage that ended in a contentious divorce, during which her ex-partner repeatedly accused her of being untrustworthy and unstable in front of friends and family. Coming from a background where she already felt academically insecure and socially underestimated, these attacks on her character were deeply humiliating and left her scanning every interaction at work and in the local art scene for signs that people were judging or talking about her. Over the next year, she spent more and more time journaling late into the night, re-reading text messages, and mentally replaying conversations at the register and at open-mic nights, gradually weaving together a tightly organized narrative about why others were behaving the way they were toward her, which she guarded fiercely despite reassurances from a few supportive peers. As her conviction hardened, conflicts with her manager and estrangement from some friends increased, and when a volunteer coordinator at an art fair gently suggested she talk to someone because her explanations for minor mishaps had become unusually intense and inflexible, Michelle reluctantly agreed to see a psychiatrist at the urging of her mother.
patient.chief_complaint: “I keep holding on to these beliefs about what people are really doing and saying about me, and I can’t let them go even when everyone tells me I’m wrong.”

S019.name: Delusions
S019.description: Fixed beliefs that do not change easily, even in the face of contradictory evidence.
S019.manifestation: For over a year now, every little thing people say or do around me—like my manager whispering with another cashier, or someone laughing near my register, or the way my ex’s friends like a post on Instagram—fits into this whole story I’ve worked out that they’ve all decided I’m crazy and untrustworthy, and no matter how many times my mom or a friend says I’m reading too much into it, I just know they’re lying to protect me or are in on it too.
